holdings.title: National-party receipt and spending: section 323(a)
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: Congress may close a demonstrated party fundraising channel used to circumvent lawful federal candidate-contribution restrictions when the government establishes an objectively grounded important corruption or circumvention interest and a close fit preserving meaningful political association. Section 323(a) satisfies that standard for national committees, including congressional campaign committees, their directly or indirectly established, financed, maintained or controlled entities, and officers or agents acting on their behalf: solicitation, receipt, direction and spending must comply with federal amount, source and reporting rules, even when the funds are designated for state or local elections.
holdings.explanation:
Lamb permits prevention based on actual resources, tacit donor understandings and relevant experience without a completed bribe, a new local study or proof of legislators' subjective reliance on particular evidence. Colorado II supplies the supported circumvention principle; Shrink Missouri and Day require close fit and meaningful use of the chosen association. Here federal-officeholder fundraising, donor credits, allocation arrangements and national-to-state transfers establish an integrated candidate-financing institution. The obligation can arise when the money is solicited or received; allocating its later use to a state project does not remove that connection.

The objection that the rule burdens the party's own independent and state expression is substantial. The restriction addresses the supported receipt channel and preserves meaningful federal fundraising and lawful individual and political-committee contributions. It does not classify all party expression as coordinated. A second unlimited account would reopen the same demonstrated channel. Ordinary access, lobbying, policy agreement, party identity, donor prominence and unequal influence alone would not establish the justification; government retains the burden on a materially different application. The lower court's broad invalidation is reversed and its residual sustaining result affirmed on this receipt-and-source ground.
holdings.precedent: Lamb is applied to supported preventive control without a completed local scandal; its separate fit requirement remains. Colorado II is applied to demonstrated circumvention, while Colorado I retains protection for genuinely independent expenditure. Shrink Missouri, Day and Mariani retain their objective-justification, meaningful-association and actual-source limits. Daggett's voluntary capped public-financing permission supplies neither an equalization power nor a public-funding mandate.

holdings.title: State and local registration, turnout and the Levin accommodation
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule:
Section 323(b) may require federal financing for voter registration from 120 days before a regularly scheduled federal election through election day, and voter identification, get-out-the-vote or generic campaign activity in an election in which a federal candidate is on the ballot. Generic activity promotes a party rather than a federal or nonfederal candidate. Covered actors include state, district and local party committees, their directly or indirectly established, financed, maintained or controlled entities, officers or agents acting for such committees or entities, and associations or similar groups of state/local candidates or officeholders. The statutory exclusions remain: public communications referring solely to a clearly identified state/local candidate that are not registration or turnout/generic activity; contributions to state/local candidates not designated for federal-election activity; state/local conventions; and grassroots materials naming or depicting only a state/local candidate.

The Levin allocation option applies only to the first two activity classes. It requires no reference to a federal candidate; no broadcast, cable or satellite cost except a communication referring solely to a clearly identified state/local candidate; compliance with state law; and no more than $10,000 from one donor to one committee in a calendar year, with controlled-person aggregation. The spending committee must raise the funds itself. Funds from another state/district/local committee, a national or national congressional committee, their representative officers or agents, or their controlled entities are excluded. The specially permitted nonfederal amounts may not be solicited, received, directed, transferred or spent by or in the name of section 323(a) or (e) actors. Joint fundraising by two or more state/district/local committees or their agents, or by a committee for one in another State, is excluded. Section 323(e)(3)'s permission to attend, speak or appear as a featured guest remains. These cumulative conditions govern that allocation option, rather than every lawful federal-fund transfer.
holdings.explanation:
Colorado II and Lamb permit safeguards against documented donor directions and transfers through shared federal-election machinery. That machinery supplies the connection here; the rule does not rest merely on a possibility that a state voter may eventually vote federally. Defined activity categories, the state-only exclusions and modified allocation preserve substantial state activity. Own fundraising and transfer restrictions prevent multiplication of the per-committee allowance into the national channel that section 323(a) closes.

The contrary argument correctly identifies burdens on local pooling and association. Day requires the government to justify those burdens rather than point to some other speaker or demand proof that the party has become silent. The demonstrated shared financing route and the confined mixed-fund option satisfy that burden on this facial record. An organizer's predominantly local purpose does not sever the actual federal-ballot mobilization connection. The district court's invalidation of these two classes and their associated Levin operation is reversed. Concrete applications that demonstrate disabling associational burdens remain governed by the same government-borne standard.
holdings.precedent: Colorado II and Lamb are applied to the identified transfer and shared-operation mechanism. Day's meaningful-chosen-association requirement remains independently binding; the accommodation does not create a universal permissible contribution amount.

holdings.title: Federal-candidate communications by parties and state officials
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: The class in section 301(20)(A)(iii), applied through section 323(b), covers a public communication referring to a clearly identified federal candidate and promoting, supporting, attacking or opposing that candidate for that office, whether or not it also identifies a state/local candidate or expressly advocates a vote. Mere mention, policy inquiry or incidental electoral effect alone does not satisfy that meaning. Public communications include broadcast, cable, satellite, newspaper, magazine, outdoor advertising, general-public political advertising, mass mailing and telephone banks. The last two categories require more than 500 identical or substantially similar mailed/faxed pieces or calls within 30 days. Section 323(f) applies the federal-funding rule to such communications by a state/local candidate or officeholder or their agent, subject to its own exception for a communication connected with that person's state/local election referring only to that person, other candidates for the same state/local office held or sought, or both.
holdings.explanation:
The candidate-for-office predicate identifies the federal financing channel. Colorado II and Lamb permit source safeguards directed to that channel; Bartlett and Clifton preserve genuine issue discussion and ordinary policy inquiries. The same source may otherwise migrate to an unrestricted state-candidate account. The statutory communication and actor conditions, together with the own-election exception, supply the required bounds.

The principal objection is that a party or state candidate speaks independently even when praising a federal candidate. This holding regulates the supported funding route without converting all such expression into coordination. The government must establish the enacted predicates and justify a materially different burden under the governing fit rule. Neither a mandatory vocabulary of electoral slogans nor a subjective-intent prosecution is adopted. The district court's sustaining judgments on class (iii) and section 323(f) are affirmed.
holdings.precedent: Bartlett supplies the distinction between electoral campaigning and incidental issue influence; Clifton preserves independent issue inquiries. Colorado I remains effective for actual independence, and Colorado II and Lamb support the separately established financing safeguard.

holdings.title: Full-salary consequence after the monthly federal-work threshold
holdings.author: O'Connor
holdings.rule: The judgment invalidating section 301(20)(A)(iv), as applied through section 323(b), is vacated and remanded. When an employee of a state, district or local party committee spends more than 25 percent of compensated time in a month on activities in connection with a federal election, the Act subjects the whole covered salary to federal financing. The government must establish that this full-payroll consequence closely fits the supported circumvention mechanism and preserves meaningful state-party association; validating the other activity classes does not establish that fit. Adequate existing evidence may suffice. If the government cannot justify the actual operation, the district court must give corresponding relief, severing applications only where statutory independence permits.
holdings.explanation:
Lamb separates proof of a legitimate preventive mechanism from justification of the burden actually imposed. Stengel's fit inquiry likewise requires examination of the challenged aggregate operation. Employees materially engaged in shared federal work present a real financing relation. That relation does not itself explain why crossing a quarter-time threshold requires federal funding of the remaining compensation.

The competing lower conclusions do not resolve this inquiry under the governing government-borne standard. The administrative advantage of preventing artificial division of staff duties must be tested against the whole-payroll burden and meaningful local-party operation. Conversely, indirect effects on state activity alone do not establish invalidity. The remand applies that standard to the actual operation and available evidence. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas directly join this ground and remedy while preferring broader invalidation.
holdings.precedent: Lamb's separate government-borne fit requirement and Stengel's operation-specific inquiry are applied. The accepted federal-election source does not settle the independent speech burden.

holdings.title: Tax-exempt recipients and federally compliant funds: section 323(d)
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: Section 323(d) survives for its nonfederal-fund applications, but solicitation, donation or direction of funds complying with federal safeguards is protected by application severance under section 401. The enacted words cover any funds; the remedy does not rewrite them as a soft-money-only definition. It covers national, state, district and local party committees, including national congressional campaign committees, entities directly or indirectly established, financed, maintained or controlled by such a committee or its agent, and officers or agents acting for the committee or entity. Covered recipients are section 501(c) organizations exempt under section 501(a), or applicants for that status, making expenditures or disbursements in connection with a federal election, including federal-election activity; and section 527 organizations other than political committees, state/district/local party committees or authorized state/local candidate committees. Independent organizational activity outside these party-channel restrictions remains protected.
holdings.explanation:
The satellite-organization record, including use of a nominal ballot organization for partisan registration, supports a substitute conduit for prohibited party money. Lamb and Colorado II allow a source-specific response to that demonstrated route. The defined recipients, representative-capacity limit and exceptions confine it.

Federally compliant solicitation and donations present a different burden. The government has not justified excluding that lawful funding channel merely because the recipient also engages in federal-election activity. Day and Mariani require attention to the chosen association; another fund operated by the recipient is not automatically an adequate substitute. Section 401 permits the unconstitutional compliant-fund applications to be severed while the nonfederal applications remain independently operative. The three Justices seeking full invalidation directly join the compliant-fund protection, but not the approval of the nonfederal residue. The lower injunction is affirmed for compliant funds and reversed for the surviving nonfederal applications.
holdings.precedent: Day and Mariani retain protection for meaningful use of the lawful chosen channel. Lamb and Colorado II support the distinct nonfederal conduit rule. Section 401 operates through application severance, not deletion of statutory coverage words.
holdings.extra_authority: All nine directly join the severed protection for federally compliant solicitation, donation and direction; only the six named sustaining Justices join the nonfederal residue.

holdings.title: Federal officeholders and candidates: section 323(e)
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule:
Section 323(e) is sustained on the federal candidate's or officeholder's own solicitation, direction, receipt, transfer or spending connection, including agents and entities directly or indirectly established, financed, maintained or controlled by, or acting on behalf of, one or more such candidates or officeholders. The federal-election branch requires federal source, amount and reporting compliance; the other-election branch imports the source restrictions and section 315(a)(1)–(3) amount limits rather than all federal reporting duties.

The own-state/local-candidacy exception applies to an individual who is or was also such a candidate, soliciting, receiving or spending solely in connection with that election, as state law permits, and referring only to that candidate, other candidates for the state/local office sought by that candidate, or both. Attendance, speaking and featured-guest participation at state/district/local-party fundraising events remain permitted. General solicitations for section 501(c) organizations exempt under section 501(a), or applying for exemption, may not specify use and exclude entities principally devoted to the defined registration, voter-identification, turnout or generic activities. Specific solicitations for those activities, or for entities principally conducting them, may be made only to individuals and for no more than $20,000 from each in a calendar year.
holdings.explanation:
The supported donor obligation attaches to the official's personal fundraising intervention, even when the recipient spends in another election. Lamb recognizes actual resources and tacit conduits without a formal earmark or a completed bribe; Mariani supplies the actual-source distinction. The record of large donations obtained and credited through federal officials supports this connection more directly than party identity or ordinary access alone.

The contrary argument treats a state-election or charitable destination as wholly unrelated to the official's federal position. It overlooks the actual requester-donor relationship. The distinct statutory branches and express candidacy, participation and charitable exceptions preserve ordinary political and charitable association. All nine adopt this particular source-and-amount safeguard. The district court's facial sustaining judgment is affirmed.
holdings.precedent: Lamb and Mariani are applied to the official's own supported fundraising relation. Colorado I and Clifton continue to protect independent expression and ordinary issue cooperation outside that relation.

holdings.title: Primary electioneering definition and treasury-funded electoral advocacy
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule:
The primary definition is sustained and the facial challenge to sections 203 and 204 rejected subject to enforceable independent-speech and nonprofit protections. Coverage requires broadcast, cable or satellite communication identifying a federal candidate within 60 days before a general, special or runoff election or 30 days before a primary, preference election, nominating convention or caucus for the office sought. For candidates other than President or Vice President, reception by at least 50,000 persons in the House district or Senate State supplies the relevant-electorate requirement. The news, commentary and editorial exception excludes facilities owned or controlled by a political party, political committee or candidate. Already covered expenditures and independent expenditures are separately excluded; qualifying regulated debates/forums and communications solely promoting them by or for their sponsors are excluded. A regulatory exemption cannot include the otherwise covered section 301(20)(A)(iii) class.

Covered corporations and unions may be required to finance genuine electoral advocacy through lawful voluntarily supported segregated funds rather than their treasuries. The statutory definition does not conclusively establish constitutionally suppressible advocacy. Under Bartlett the whole message, context, actual audience request and financing must be examined; a reasonable nonelectoral interpretation remains constitutionally material. Election proximity, candidate identification, potential voter influence or opposition to a legislator's policy alone cannot defeat genuine independent issue advocacy. Actual electoral advocacy requires no rigid slogan list. Government must justify the electoral and financing connection. Genuine press activity and natural persons' independent political expenditures retain their constitutional protection.
holdings.explanation:
Austin remains authority for the surviving treasury-funded electoral-advocacy setting. Its concern with resources accumulated through the commercial structure, rather than voluntary political support, is distinct from equalizing influence or labeling every independent supporter corrupt. The record of commercial and union financing of candidate-centered broadcasts through nominal issue sponsors, the objective coverage conditions and meaningful voluntary funding routes support the facial result. Corporate form and a nominal alternative fund alone would not suffice.

Bartlett protects genuine independent issue discussion; Maine Right to Life rejects reliance on a mandatory set of electoral words while retaining definite coverage. A request to contact a senator about impending legislation therefore requires constitutional examination different from an appeal to replace the senator in the election. The genuine-issue examples and disputed advertising estimates do not establish that every covered message may be suppressed. The facial judgment preserves enforceable application protection rather than resolving future advertisements in advance. Beaumont's direct-contribution holding cannot supply a rule equating independent expenditure with candidate financing. The primary-definition invalidation is reversed; section 203 operates under that definition and these constitutional limits instead of the district court's enlarged fallback.
holdings.precedent: Austin is retained within its independent electoral-treasury setting. Bartlett's genuine-issue protection and Maine Right to Life's definite, non-slogan-only approach remain effective. Beaumont and Stengel's direct-contribution holdings are distinguished. Buckley and Colorado I retain independent-expenditure protection.

holdings.title: Functional nonprofit protection and the statutory withdrawal
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule:
Withdrawal of the statutory nonprofit exception under section 204 does not withdraw MCFL and Day's constitutional protection for a functionally qualifying voluntary political association. The claimant must establish its actual characteristics: economic claimants, material commercial accumulation, material corporate or union financing or control, and whether advocacy funds reflect voluntary political support. Incidental commercial activity or an imperfect formal refusal policy alone does not defeat protection; tax status and ideological purpose alone do not establish it.

The separate statutory exception in section 203 concerns section 501(c)(4) entities, including applicants, and section 527(e)(1) organizations using exclusively funds provided directly by individual citizens, nationals or lawful permanent residents. Prohibited-entity-origin funds do not qualify. Direct or indirect payment by a prohibited entity invokes attribution; a section 501(c)(4) entity with business receipts or prohibited-source funds must use the individual-only section 304(f)(2)(E) account to avoid that attribution. Contracts count and tax-law restrictions remain. Section 204 withdraws that statutory exception for communications distributed from a television or radio station or cable/satellite television provider, with the relevant-electorate requirement for candidates other than President or Vice President. Outside the constitutional class, the withdrawal survives by the six-Justice treasury coalition.
holdings.explanation:
MCFL protects the distinct voluntary political association; Day requires a functional inquiry rather than a literal paperwork checklist. Stengel preserves the distinction between independent expression and direct candidate gifts. The government's anti-conduit argument has force when material business financing or control is present. It does not answer an association whose incidental receipts or formal defects leave its advocacy resources genuinely voluntary.

The lower decree's nonprofit protection is retained and modified to state this functional class. Application to an organization depends on its own characteristics and communication. All nine join the constitutional protection. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas continue to oppose the expanded treasury trigger outside that class; their join here does not sustain that separate restriction.
holdings.precedent: MCFL is applied through Day's actual-characteristics protection, including incidental-receipt and formal-defect limits. Stengel continues to distinguish this independent-spending protection from direct candidate contributions.
holdings.extra_authority: All nine join functional constitutional protection. Only Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer join survival of the statutory withdrawal outside that class.

holdings.title: The enacted fallback and its actual activation
holdings.author: O'Connor
holdings.rule: The district court's fallback declaration and deletion of the final narrowing condition are vacated. The statute activates the fallback only if a final judicial decision holds the primary definition constitutionally insufficient. The Court sustains the primary scheme on the grounds and with the protections stated here, so the condition is not met. The fallback's text remains complete: a broadcast, cable or satellite communication must promote, support, attack or oppose a candidate and have no plausible meaning other than an exhortation to vote for or against a specific candidate; section 100.22(b)'s interpretation and application are preserved. The fallback contains neither the primary time windows nor its geographic threshold.
holdings.explanation: Section 401 permits severance of provisions or applications, but does not authorize deletion of a limiting condition to enlarge regulation. The lower remedy removed Congress's cumulative restriction. Because the Court's actual primary disposition does not activate the alternative, the lower alternative declaration has no present operative function. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas also oppose deletion of the limiter, but their preferred primary treasury disposition would require a complete backup analysis. Their conditional construction is stated in their separate writing rather than treated as an operative rule. Stone-Zsela agrees with this fallback disposition without adding a ground.
holdings.precedent: Maine Right to Life's cumulative contextual construction remains applicable in its own setting. The fallback remains inactive under its enacted trigger.

holdings.title: Actual spending coordination and enforceable requested resources
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: Sections 202 and 214(a) survive facial review where actual cooperation, consultation, concert, request, suggestion or another legally sufficient spending connection supplies candidate or party campaign resources. A written agreement or formal collaboration is unnecessary. Shared objectives, endorsement, ordinary policy inquiries, party affiliation, access, vendor identity or former employment alone do not establish coordination. An enforceable coordinated purchase commitment that already supplies an actual requested campaign resource may be classified as a contribution and expenditure before airing or payment; all nine directly support that financial-resource proposition.
holdings.explanation:
Colorado I protects actual independence; Colorado II and Lamb recognize real resources and tacit conduits under the contribution standard. Akins makes actual candidate financing decisive rather than an organizational label or slogan requirement. Clifton protects policy inquiries and independently edited publications absent the necessary spending relation.

The objection that no formal agreement exists fails because the campaign can receive an actual financial substitute through an informal arrangement. Conversely, ordinary dialogue does not supply that substitute. A binding purchase arranged to provide the campaign's advertising can transfer the benefit before performance. This differs from publishing the private plans for a separate independent message. The January coordination rule's payment, content and conduct structure and policy-inquiry safe harbor rebut the premise of a regulatory vacuum; the regulation's applications are not adjudicated through this facial statutory holding.

The facial sustaining judgment is affirmed by six. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas join the enforceable requested-resource application and inquiry/identity exclusions but seek a broader present declaration protecting party-owned joint expression and independent editorial activity. Their more protective remedy does not become a full join in the facial approval.
holdings.precedent: Colorado I, Colorado II, Lamb and Akins retain their distinct independence, contribution and actual-resource functions. Clifton's ordinary-inquiry and independent-editing boundary remains. No contribution classification arises from party identity alone.
holdings.extra_authority: All nine join the enforceable requested-resource contract proposition and ordinary-inquiry/identity exclusions. Only the six named sustaining Justices join the complete facial sustaining ground and remedy.

holdings.title: Sections 211 and 214(d): the actual statutory definitions
holdings.author: O'Connor
holdings.rule: The section 211 facial definition claim is rejected: statutory independent expenditure requires express advocacy and absence of concert, cooperation, request or suggestion with a candidate or the specified political-party connection. Falling outside that definition does not itself eliminate independent constitutional protection. The section 214(d) amendment challenge is also rejected because incorporation of FECA's contribution and expenditure definitions did not newly enact the preexisting direct-or-indirect-payment language.
holdings.explanation: The definition and the constitutional burden imposed on particular conduct are different questions. Colorado I and Clifton preserve independence and editorial protection even when a statutory label does not itself decide the constitutional question. Lamb permits regulation of actual requested resources without formal agreement. Incorporating definitions does not turn every policy communication into a contribution or create a new enactment of old words. These statutory grounds resolve the presented theories within the coordination disposition. Stone-Zsela concurs in the disposition without adding a statutory ground.
holdings.precedent: Colorado I and Clifton remain independent constitutional protections; Lamb continues to permit genuine financial-resource treatment. The definitions neither broaden nor repeal those holdings.

holdings.title: Completed repeal and unspecified regulatory applications
holdings.author: O'Connor
holdings.rule: The section 214(b) regulatory-vacuum theory is dismissed as moot after the replacement rules became effective February 3, 2003. The challenge to unspecified applications of section 214(c)'s rulemaking command is unripe. The command removes an agreement or formal-collaboration prerequisite and requires treatment of republication, common vendors, former employees and substantial discussions; it does not itself classify every contact as coordinated. Advisory opinions remain permissive.
holdings.explanation: The replacement rule ended the claimed unregulated interval. Its conjunctive spending predicates and policy-inquiry safe harbor also distinguish the generalized future-application claim from a present protected communication forced into coordination. Maine Right to Life and Lee recognize that an actual civil duty can support review; neither exhaustion of an advisory procedure nor a criminal penalty is required. National Park Hospitality's nonbinding-policy setting does not erase an operative statutory duty. Barnhart requires an actual delegated assignment rather than presumed power to rewrite a statute. The threshold disposition concerns the completed vacuum and unspecified applications, leaving an appropriate concrete regulatory challenge available.
holdings.precedent: Maine Right to Life's permissive advisory procedure and Lee's present-civil-duty rule remain. National Park Hospitality is distinguished by its nonbinding policy; Barnhart requires an actual statutory assignment and its lawful exercise.

holdings.title: The reciprocal party choice: section 213
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: Section 213's postnomination election-cycle choice is invalid as a unit: exercise of the special coordinated-party allowance cannot require surrender of genuinely independent expenditure, or vice versa. The single-committee and transfer, assignment and receipt restrictions implement that reciprocal choice and fall with it. The preexisting ordinary contribution and special coordinated-allowance rules remain operative under their lawful limits.
holdings.explanation:
Colorado I requires actual independence or coordination, not a conclusive status presumption from the party's other spending. Colorado II permits supported restrictions on genuine coordination but does not authorize extinguishing the independent option. Day and Lamb require meaningful use of the chosen association. The ordinary $5,000 multicandidate contribution route remains available after independent spending, yet that alternative does not justify conditioning another lawful allowance on abandoning independent speech.

The government's strongest argument is that earlier coordination makes later independence unreliable and that the allowance is optional. Genuine coordination can be proved and regulated on its facts; the supported record supplies no fitted basis for the conclusive reciprocal choice. Section 401 cannot create a different one-sided option. The lower invalidation is affirmed for everyone governed by the statutory choice.
holdings.precedent: Colorado I's independence rule and Colorado II's actual-coordination limit are applied. Day and Lamb preserve meaningful association in the reciprocal choice presented here.

holdings.title: Ordinary electioneering-finance reports
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule:
Ordinary section 201 reporting survives the facial challenge. Government must establish a material connection between the information demanded and a legitimate electoral-information or source-tracing interest. A claimant seeking protective relief must substantiate the asserted associational injury; government retains justification of remaining exposure. Direct production or airing costs aggregating more than $10,000 in a calendar year trigger a report within 24 hours of each disclosure date and each later additional over-$10,000 aggregate. The report identifies the disburser, activity directors/controllers, records custodian and nonindividual principal place of business; disbursements over $200 and recipients; and relevant elections and candidates known or to be identified. Donors of $1,000 or more are identified over the period from the first day of the preceding calendar year through disclosure.

When the communication is paid from the qualifying segregated account consisting solely of direct contributions for electioneering communications by individual citizens, nationals or lawful permanent residents, donor disclosure is confined to that account, which may also be used for other purposes. Otherwise the statute reaches qualifying contributors to the disburser, not merely earmarked advertising donors. Reporting supplements other duties and preserves tax-law definitions. A demonstrated reasonable probability of threats, harassment or reprisals supports protective relief; disproportionate concrete associational burdens remain reviewable.
holdings.explanation:
Buckley and Brown permit materially connected financial disclosure with supported reprisal protection. Stengel, Akins and Mariani distinguish actual financing and truthful sources from a prohibition on the message. The defined major candidate-focused broadcasts, finite reporting events, donor thresholds and qualifying-account option provide a substantial informational relation. They permit voters to identify who pays for organized election-period advocacy and to trace financing through intermediaries.

McIntyre's protection of anonymous individual pamphlets and Bartlett's rejection of an indefinite full-committee regime do not make every paid-broadcast report invalid whenever the message lacks express advocacy. The account option and substantial funding-pool relation answer this facial claim while leaving actual injury review available. A reporting duty supplies no authority to prohibit the independent message or expose unrelated association records. The informational relation supplies the sufficient common ground. The ordinary-reporting judgment is affirmed, and any primary-definition restraint inconsistent with that independent reporting operation is reversed.
holdings.precedent: Buckley/Brown's supported-reprisal protection remains. Stengel, Akins and Mariani support financial-source reporting. McIntyre's individual anonymity and Bartlett's issue-expression and full-committee limits are preserved and distinguished.

holdings.title: Executed contracts under section 304(f)(5)
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: The complete severance of section 304(f)(5) is reversed. An executed binding purchase obligation may be treated as a reportable disbursement before payment. Under the effective rule public distribution triggers the initial report after the aggregate threshold is exceeded; that report may include executed obligations for other communications that have not yet aired. The duty concerns actual financial commitments, with the same statutory thresholds, government-borne material-information connection and supported associational protections, rather than negotiations or preliminary drafts. All nine agree that unpaid obligations for an already disseminated communication are reportable.
holdings.explanation:
Stengel and Akins support accounting for actual financing; Mariani supplies source transparency. An executed purchase is an existing financial transaction even while payment or a separate airing remains in the future. Reporting amounts, financing and pertinent elections does not require publication of the full script or permission to speak.

The strongest objection is disclosure of a separate message's confidential preparation when another advertisement airs. That is a real burden. The six-Justice Court concludes that the binding commitment, finite aggregate and financial character of the report supply the required relation on this facial record; cancellation possibilities and strategic privacy do not themselves defeat it. Concrete reprisal and disproportionate-burden claims remain available. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas would protect only the separate unbroadcast application, preserving reports for public communications and narrowing rather than affirming the district's complete-clause severance.
holdings.precedent: Stengel, Akins and Mariani are applied to actual obligations. Clifton's independent editorial protection remains distinct.
holdings.extra_authority: All nine join reporting unpaid obligations for an already disseminated communication. Only the six named sustaining Justices approve reporting executed contracts for separate unbroadcast communications.

holdings.title: The section 212 advance-reporting challenge
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: Rejection of the presented section 212 challenge is affirmed on the actual-financial-obligation ground, rather than a separate ripeness holding. Government must justify the material electoral-information or source-tracing connection, with supported associational relief and justification of remaining exposure as stated for section 201. Statutory reports are due within 24 hours for $1,000-or-more independent-expenditure aggregates after the twentieth day but more than 24 hours before election, and within 48 hours for $10,000-or-more aggregates up to and including the twentieth day, with reports for successive corresponding aggregates for the same election. Contracts are included; receipt constitutes filing for the $1,000 report. The effective rule measures the deadlines from public distribution or dissemination.
holdings.explanation:
The statutory contract language is not eliminated simply because the agency administers a dissemination trigger. Lee and Maine Right to Life recognize operative civil duties; National Park Hospitality does not convert them into nonbinding policy. The Court's section 201 conclusion that a real binding financial obligation may be reported before payment and before a separate airing answers the parallel facial advance-reporting objection. The finite financial relation and supported associational protections supply the basis for rejecting additional injunctive relief. The Court does not establish a separate general ripeness rule through that resolution.

Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas would reach and protect the statute's advance application to an independent message before dissemination, while preserving ordinary reports and the protective distribution-based regulation. Their proposed remedy concerns the broader statutory obligation, not an assertion that the agency presently demands an advance report contrary to its rule.
holdings.precedent: The actual-obligation reasoning of the section 201 holding governs this parallel claim. Lee and Maine Right to Life preserve review of concrete civil duties; National Park Hospitality's policy setting supplies no contrary categorical bar.

holdings.title: Lowest-unit-rate certification: section 305
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: The section 305 challenge is dismissed without prejudice because these claimants have not established the required concrete present rate/certification conflict. McConnell's next identified exposure is his 2008 election; the other identified candidate circumstances do not establish the necessary current dispute. Congressional permission to sue does not itself supply Article III injury. The dismissal leaves the condition's constitutional merits unresolved for want of a justiciable claim.
holdings.explanation:
Lujan and Raines require concrete personal injury, causation and likely redress at the actual litigation stage. Lee recognizes that civil loss of a benefit or a purchase-time condition can injure a speaker; a criminal sanction is unnecessary. The supplied future plans and candidate-specific circumstances nevertheless do not establish the present conflict required here.

The statute requires certification at purchase. An opponent reference can retain preferred-rate eligibility through the television alternative—candidate image and readable identifying, approval and authorized-committee-payment statement simultaneously for at least four seconds at the end—or the radio alternative, the candidate's own identifying, office and approval statement. Noncompliance affects that and subsequent covered broadcasts during the relevant 45-/60-day periods. The Court's threshold disposition does not depend on finding that every station will charge a higher rate. Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer regard the intended conduct and present campaign planning as sufficient and would reach the merits; the Court requires the more concrete claimant-specific showing.
holdings.precedent: Lujan and Raines are applied to the actual temporal and personal nexus. Lee's recognition of civil-duty and lost-benefit injury is preserved; section 403 permission does not replace Article III.

holdings.title: Paul: amended ceilings, unchanged limits and the available remedy
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: Paul's section 307 candidate-contribution and comparative Press Clause claims, and the challenge to unchanged nonparty-PAC ceilings and indexing differences, are dismissed without prejudice to the proper review route. Willing-donor and campaign-receipt allegations establish a distinct asserted injury. But section 403 review of BCRA and its amendments cannot furnish the requested removal of the preexisting FECA restrictions: invalidating an increase or indexing amendment leaves the older limit and media treatment in place. This action cannot remove that restraint; dismissal leaves proper section 437h review available under its own requirements.
holdings.explanation:
Lujan requires likely redress as well as injury. Mariani preserves the statutory constitutional-review route, including its actual eligibility, substantiality and certification requirements. Paul's donor evidence is not Adams's relative-influence theory. Recognizing that evidence does not expand the legal consequences available from striking BCRA's increase.

The contrary argument treats the changed dollar figure as reenactment of the whole ceiling and therefore seeks deletion of the underlying restraint. The text of section 403 and the continued FECA prohibition do not support that remedy in this action. Raising or indexing other allowances likewise does not authorize judicial enlargement of the unchanged PAC ceiling. The dismissal resolves the action/remedy defect while preserving a proper challenge to the real restraint; it is not a merits adjudication of Paul's distinct Press theory.
holdings.precedent: Lujan's injury and redressability elements remain separate. Mariani's section 437h route is applied without automatic certification or conversion of this direct appeal into review of every FECA restriction.

holdings.title: Adams: increased limits and particularized competitive injury
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: The Adams increased-limit claim is dismissed without prejudice. The asserted classwide dilution of electoral influence and deterrence of future candidacies do not establish a concrete, imminent personal competitive disadvantage traceable to the particular challenged increase and likely redressable by restoring the older ceilings. This claimant-specific disposition preserves ordinary competitor standing when its actual requirements are established.
holdings.explanation:
Lujan and Raines demand a supported personal nexus, not simply a prediction about the political environment. The testimony and projections concerning fundraising disparity are acknowledged. Uniform increased permissions, private donor choices and contemplated future races do not on this theory establish the requisite particular statutory injury. Restoring the prior ceilings might alter fundraising conditions without redressing a particular plaintiff's Article III injury.

The strongest alternative treats documented competition as concrete economic injury. Such a theory can be legally serious even when no substantive right to equal influence exists; standing cannot be denied merely because a claim would lose on the merits. Akins also shows that widely shared injury can remain concrete. The defect here is the actual individual and causal showing, distinct from Paul's existing receipt restraint.
holdings.precedent: Lujan and Raines are applied to particularization and causation; Akins's recognition of concrete shared injury remains. No categorical competitor-standing bar follows.

holdings.title: Presented self-financing challenges: sections 304, 316 and 319
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: The presented self-financing challenges are dismissed without prejudice because these claimants have not established an actual or imminent triggering candidate race. A self-financing candidate, an opponent potentially entitled to an increased allowance, an additional opponent and a party committee have distinct statutory positions; they cannot supply one another's injury. The constitutional merits of the presented scheme remain undecided for this Article III reason.
holdings.explanation:
Day and Daggett demonstrate that a legal response to protected expenditure can burden speech before a transfer is complete. They do not supply a claimant subject to this different statutory formula. The lower record's claimant posture establishes no presently triggering race, and party concerns about supporting candidates equally do not establish actual adverse treatment under that formula.

The Senate mechanism begins at $150,000 plus four cents per voting-age resident, with twice/four-times/ten-times bands, threefold/sixfold allowances and the highest band's coordinated-party relaxation. Section 316 adjusts opposition funds by half the gross-receipts advantage using specified June 30/December 31 measurements. The House scheme begins above $350,000, with tripled individual limits, its own receipts rule and a 100-percent cap; the Senate acceptance cap is 110 percent. Increased acceptance follows notice, attributable permission ends when the opponent withdraws, and unspent excess must be returned within 50 days. These qualifications underscore why the actual claimant and election matter. The existing declarations, notices and distinct personal-loan provision are statutory context, not newly presented independent claims.
holdings.precedent: Lujan and Raines supply the claimant-specific threshold. Day and Daggett's different public-financing positions do not determine the merits or create injury under this formula.

holdings.title: Sponsor identification: section 311
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: Section 311's challenged extension of sponsor identification to electioneering communications and other covered non-express advocacy is sustained. Government must justify the material electoral-information or source-tracing connection; a claimant must substantiate protective injury while government retains justification of remaining exposure. Factual designation of the responsible sponsor has that relation to the covered paid communication and is distinct from compelled ideological endorsement. This on-message duty has its own scope and does not acquire section 201's $10,000 reporting threshold.
holdings.explanation:
Stengel distinguishes organizational campaign-finance identification from McIntyre's ordinary individual leaflet. Clifton preserves accurate disclosure under separately valid authority. The source statement allows the audience to identify the payer while leaving the message's substance and volume to the speaker. The claim that every identification requirement must end at express advocacy therefore fails.

Candidate or authorized-speaker identification differs from the other-speaker responsible-for-content and connected-organization statements. The enacted box, type, contrast, image, voice, approval and duration specifications are retained as statutory context; the preserved challenge concerns the extension rather than each design detail independently. Supported reprisals and disproportionate concrete burdens remain subject to the governing associational protection. Thomas would protect on-message anonymity for independent genuine-issue broadcasts because the distinct command lacks the external report's monetary threshold; he preserves definite electoral-advocacy and valid candidate-finance attribution. The other eight affirm rejection of the extension challenge.
holdings.precedent: Stengel's source-identification distinction and Clifton's separate-disclosure reservation are applied. McIntyre's individual-pamphlet protection remains, and Bartlett's prohibition/full-committee boundary is not converted into a universal reporting boundary.

holdings.title: The complete minor-contribution ban: section 318
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: Section 318's prohibition on contributions to candidates and contributions or donations to party committees by persons seventeen or younger is invalid in full. The categorical exclusion, including voluntary gifts from a minor's own resources, is not closely fitted to preventing adults from using children as false donors. Existing lawful amount, source, voluntariness and true-source restrictions remain enforceable.
holdings.explanation:
Tinker recognizes minors' expressive rights; Buckley and Shrink Missouri supply the contribution standard. Day, Russell and Lamb require meaningful use of the chosen association. Mariani independently permits enforcement against false names and knowing reimbursement. Volunteering and independent expenditure are not adequate answers to the complete exclusion of the contribution channel.

The government invokes parental influence, evasion risk and an administrable age line. Those concerns support actual attribution and conduit rules but do not fit a prohibition reaching every genuine voluntary gift and lawful amount. Difficulty enforcing a narrower rule does not itself justify that sweep. The holding does not depend on a finding that parental evasion never occurs. Section 401 cannot enact a replacement age, earnings or consent condition. The lower invalidation is affirmed for everyone governed by the ban; complete First Amendment relief makes the alternative federalism and equality grounds unnecessary to the decree.
holdings.precedent: Buckley and Shrink Missouri's contribution fit standard is applied, with Day, Russell and Lamb's chosen-channel protection. Mariani's true-source restrictions remain independently enforceable. Tinker supports the existence of minors' rights without replacing the contribution inquiry.

holdings.title: Broadcaster records of political requests: section 504
holdings.author: Stone-Zsela
holdings.rule: Section 504 survives the facial challenge in full. Government must justify the information's material electoral or broadcast-accountability connection; supported concrete protective injury and justification of remaining exposure remain material. Licensees must maintain for public inspection records of accepted and rejected requests to buy broadcast time by or for a legally qualified candidate for public office, or for a message about a political matter of national importance, including a legally qualified candidate, a federal election or a national legislative issue of public importance. Required fields include acceptance/rejection, charged rate, airing date/time, time class and pertinent candidate/office, election or issue. Candidate requests identify the candidate, authorized committee and treasurer; other requests identify purchaser, contact name/address/telephone and chief executive officers or executive-committee/board members. Information must be placed in the file as soon as possible and retained for at least two years.
holdings.explanation:
Candidate-request files permit comparison of access, rates, time classes and placement, including refusals. A purchaser's own report does not reveal every rejected request or the station's treatment. Federal-candidate and election requests have both electoral-information and licensee-accountability functions. National-political and legislative requests have the latter function even when the message is not candidate advocacy. The rule is therefore not confined to completed purchases, federal candidates or section 201's threshold.

Stengel and Akins distinguish independently justified financial records from suppression of expression; Clifton preserves editorial independence. The government's distinct licensee function, actual request predicate and enumerated fields establish the relation here. Analogous administrative experience bears on fit without conclusively establishing constitutionality. The substantial objection is public exposure of unbroadcast strategy and association. Actual requests and refusals remain relevant distributor conduct, and the records do not require the full script. Supported concrete burdens remain reviewable without assuming a confidentiality procedure that has not been established.

Scalia and Kennedy would retain the entire new-duty injunction. Thomas supports candidate requests, including refusals, and aired noncandidate federal-candidate/election records, but would protect unaired noncandidate requests and issue-only files lacking that electoral relation. Seven thus sustain the first two applications; six sustain the remaining applications. The complete facial invalidation is reversed.
holdings.precedent: Stengel and Akins support connected transaction information, while Clifton and McIntyre preserve distinct editorial and anonymity interests. Existing administrative practice is evidence of fit rather than an independently adjudicated constitutional safe harbor.
holdings.extra_authority: Thomas additionally joins the candidate-request branch, including refusals, and aired noncandidate federal-candidate/election records, making seven for those applications. The six named Justices join the other applications and the complete reversal.

holdings.title: The independent general-press and media-exemption theories
holdings.author: O'Connor
holdings.rule: The categorical claim that candidate campaigns and political organizations become immune from otherwise valid financing, source-reporting or sponsorship restrictions by describing themselves as the general press is rejected. The news/commentary/editorial exemption likewise does not automatically invalidate BCRA. Press freedom extends to noninstitutional speakers, while actual candidate receipts, paid advocacy purchases and independent news activity remain distinct regulated functions.
holdings.explanation:
McIntyre protects a noninstitutional publisher. Bellotti prevents exclusion of nonmedia speakers from First Amendment protection. Neither transforms donated campaign resources into the publisher's independent expenditure. Stengel, Akins and Mariani retain rules for actual financing and true sources; Clifton protects genuine independent editorial work. The statutory ownership/control limit and actual news function must be honored.

The alternative would treat every regulation of communicative finance as editorial licensing or require candidates and independent news facilities to receive identical financing treatment. That erases the activity-based distinctions these authorities preserve. The Court rejects the requested wholesale declarations within the live BCRA claims, leaving concrete discriminatory or independent-expression applications subject to their governing standards. Paul's separate section 307 route dismissal remains a nonmerits disposition.
holdings.precedent: Bellotti and McIntyre retain full expressive protection for noninstitutional publishers. Stengel, Akins, Clifton and Mariani supply the distinct financing, editorial and source functions rather than institutional press supremacy.

holdings.title: Standing of directly regulated parties to challenge federal allocation
holdings.author: O'Connor
holdings.rule: Parties directly restricted in their own fundraising and spending may raise the presented affirmative-power and associated reserved-power objections. Their own financial duties and exposure establish personal injury, enforcement supplies causation, and relief from those duties supplies redress. A State plaintiff is unnecessary to this own-command challenge. The prudential third-party bar adopted by one district judge does not defeat it.
holdings.explanation:
Lujan requires personal injury rather than a particular constitutional label. Lopez adjudicated a regulated person's source objection; Printz's jurisdictional holding distinguishes commands imposed on the plaintiffs from obligations imposed only on others. New York's allocation rule is not cured by state consent. Guillen reserved the distinct private Tenth Amendment question and establishes neither a categorical permission nor a categorical prohibition.

Tennessee Electric involved competition under nonexclusive franchises, rather than a federal prohibition directly binding the claimant's conduct. Its absent-State language does not foreclose this direct claim. The contrary characterization as representation of absent sovereign preferences overlooks the plaintiffs' own imposed financial restraints. This holding concerns directly injured regulated parties and leaves a claimant asserting only a State's independent institutional injury outside the question decided.
holdings.precedent: Lujan and Printz are applied to the plaintiffs' own duties. Guillen's reserved question remains reserved beyond this direct-regulation setting. Tennessee Electric is distinguished by its competitive-injury setting.

holdings.title: Affirmative federal election authority across the challenged Title I classes
holdings.author: O'Connor
holdings.rule:
Article I, section 4 authorizes fitted financial safeguards for congressional elections; presidential safeguards rest separately on the national protective authority recognized in Burroughs and Voting Rights Coalition, implemented through the Necessary and Proper Clause. Supported circumvention channels and shared federal-election operations may be reached despite state-election uses. Each challenged Title I class falls within that affirmative authority, while speech fit remains independently necessary.

The actual national-party institution supplies section 323(a)'s receipt channel, including nominally local uses. The 120-day registration and federal-ballot turnout/generic classes concern shared federal machinery; Levin own-fundraising, aggregation and transfer conditions protect the bounded allocation alternative. Class (iii) and section 323(f) concern support or opposition to a candidate for federal office, with their actual exclusions. Class (iv) concerns employees materially engaged in federal-election work, although the whole-salary speech burden requires the separate remand. Section 323(d)'s defined election-spending recipients and party routes supply a federal-financing subject even for compliant funds whose prohibition fails the separate fit test. Section 323(e)'s official-requester relationship supplies the federal connection despite another election's ultimate benefit.
holdings.explanation:
Voting Rights Coalition supplies the distinct congressional and presidential sources and preserves state qualifications. Smiley and Siebold support shared electoral administration; Burroughs protects the national executive election. Thornton and Cook distinguish genuine electoral administration from altering the constitutional representative relationship. The actual financing, solicitation and shared-operation mechanisms—not the possibility that local politics might eventually affect Washington—support these classes.

The strongest contrary argument invokes an off-year state expenditure, local campaign purpose, proportional staff accounting or state-authorized pooling. A local destination does not erase the actual federal solicitation or shared-operation mechanism. Proportional payroll and pooling burdens raise serious speech-fit questions, which remain independently governed by the dispositions above. Section 323(d)'s source authority likewise does not justify forbidding compliant money. Lopez, Holston and Ho reinforce identification of an actual constitutional mechanism; their Commerce Clause element is not transplanted into election law. This source holding rejects wholesale Title I invalidation without curing any independently invalid speech burden. The preserved state-only exceptions, candidate-for-office meanings and official-solicitation accommodations limit its reach.
holdings.precedent: Voting Rights Coalition, Smiley, Siebold and Burroughs supply the election-specific sources. Thornton and Cook preserve qualifications and representative-structure limits. Lopez, Holston and Ho supply source discipline by analogy without creating an interstate-commerce element or an alternative commerce holding.

holdings.title: Reserved state electoral authority and direct private regulation
holdings.author: O'Connor
holdings.rule: Otherwise authorized Title I restrictions do not violate the asserted reserved-state-power or Tenth Amendment limit merely because they restrict private financing that a State permits. They directly regulate the identified parties, candidates and fundraising actors. They neither require a state legislature to enact a code nor assign a state executive a general program governing others, and they leave state qualifications, offices, election calendars and administration intact. This conclusion depends on the established affirmative source and the surviving speech limits.
holdings.explanation:
New York and Condon distinguish source-supported direct regulation from compulsory state government of others. The differing Printz positions addressed imposed state administration; this private-finance arrangement does not require sustaining such an administrative command. Voting Rights Coalition separately recognizes election-specific authority while preserving state qualifications.

The contrary theory treats state campaign finance as categorically immune because it concerns state self-government. That interest does not remove an actual federal-election or federal-official financing connection. State permission to give more cannot defeat an otherwise valid federal restraint; supremacy follows after, not before, constitutional validity is established. The Court therefore rejects the wholesale structural injunction while preserving each separate speech remedy.
holdings.precedent: New York and Condon retain their direct-regulation/compulsory-government distinction. Neither the actual Printz holding nor its structural separate position is enlarged to prohibit this different arrangement. Voting Rights Coalition preserves state qualifications and the source-specific election rule.

holdings.title: Surviving party classifications and the racial-impact alternative
holdings.author: O'Connor
holdings.rule: The facial equal-protection objection to the surviving party-specific rules fails because their demonstrated institutional fundraising, donor-credit and transfer relationships justify the relevant distinctions. Genuine resource and conduit differences can support different treatment; a party label alone cannot. Separately, all eight Associate Justices reject the Thompson racial-impact theory as presented: Valeria requires an actual racial classification, deliberate proxy or racially selective political barrier, while this theory identifies demographic consequences of a uniform federal-candidate solicitation rule rather than that trigger.
holdings.explanation:
The classification inquiry uses the actual financing-channel differences supporting the surviving provisions, not a declaration that all parties are corrupt or a power to equalize influence. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas seek their wider relief on speech grounds and identify no additional equality remedy beyond it; they accept the narrower actual-resource distinction.

Valeria requires attention to structural racial barriers without making hostility indispensable in every case. Disparate demographic impact alone does not establish such a barrier here. The presented uniform solicitation restriction supplies no supported racial classification, deliberate proxy or race-defined relocation of access. The Court resolves the actual theory without transforming a neutral label into immunity for a proved discriminatory mechanism.
holdings.precedent: Day, Lamb and the governing financing decisions preserve actual rather than label-based distinctions. Valeria's racial-classification, proxy or selective-barrier rule is applied; an animus-only substitute is rejected.
holdings.extra_authority: The five named Associates directly join rejection of the surviving party-classification theory. All eight Associates join the distinct Thompson racial-impact holding. Stone-Zsela concurs in both dispositions without adding a ground.

holdings.title: Definite coverage and the separately preserved breadth objections
holdings.author: O'Connor
holdings.rule: The presented facial vagueness theories fail within the adopted meanings: the primary medium, time, candidate and electorate triggers are ascertainable; candidate promotion or opposition concerns the candidate for that office; and coordination requires an actual spending relation. Ordinary issue discussion, mere reference and incidental influence do not become the missing statutory connection. Clarity and constitutional breadth remain distinct inquiries.
holdings.explanation:
Bartlett requires definite coverage and protection for genuine issue discussion. Maine Right to Life supplies cumulative attention to what the message actually communicates, and Clifton preserves ordinary inquiries. Greenville distinguishes contextual notice from an independent branch lacking an enforceable standard. Here the identified predicates provide the standard within their adopted scope; an absence of formal agreement does not abolish the spending connection.

A clear category can still burden protected speech. The particular speech objections and remedies above therefore remain necessary despite rejection of the vagueness theory. The inactive fallback retains its entire cumulative limiter. This holding does not approve an unspecified regulation or an all-influence contact rule.
holdings.precedent: Bartlett, Maine Right to Life and Clifton supply the actual coverage limits. Greenville's distinction between contextual notice and an independent branch lacking an operative standard remains effective.

holdings.title: Intervenor standing in the existing adversarial action
holdings.author: O'Connor
holdings.rule: The intervenor-defendants' independent standing is not decided because the FEC is properly before the Court and advances the same position and relief. That additional question is unnecessary to resolve this existing adversarial action.
holdings.explanation: The present parties supply the live controversy. Section 403(b)'s intervention provision therefore requires no independent-standing adjudication on this posture. The Court resolves the shared-position setting before it.
holdings.precedent: Ordinary injury and remedial requirements remain applicable to the actual claim and relief.
